newsitem.title: UK: Less need for hull surveys - Salvage Association.
newsitem.headline: Less need for hull surveys - Salvage Association.

text.p: Hull underwriters have less reason for concern about ships' structures than in the early 1990s, the Salvage Association said on Friday.
The Salvage Association, which is the technical arm of the London marine insurance market, said hull underwriters have less cause to insist on condition surveys before insuring vessels.
Chairman Trevor Hart said: "The major structural failures to tankers and bulk carriers that the Salvage Association so frequently reported some years ago are less in evidence."
The association said the number of ship condition surveys it carried out for underwriters had fallen from a peak of more than 800 in 1993 to an estimated 200 over 1997.

This was due to an almost complete reduction in the number of full structural surveys it is carrying out due to the renewed vigour of classification society inspections and tougher port state controls, Hart said. Condition surveys are less rigorous than structural surveys.
However, Hart also pointed to the state of the insurance market in having an effect on the reduction of surveys carried out by the Salvage Association.

A rise in deductibles, the minimum excess charge for claims, meant less claims were being made while the number of major casualties had fallen off from their peak in the 1990s when major losses, such as the Piper Alpha offshore rig, badly hit the market.
This had led to softer insurance markets within which less emphasis might be put on risk reduction.
The number of damage instructions to the Salvage Association from underwriters has also fallen since 1990 -from more than 9,000 a year to less than 4,000 in 1996.
However, Hart warned there was continuing concern about claims for damage to ships' machinery, often resulting from poor maintenance.
"The skills of some superintendents and their engineroom crews are questionable," he said and added, "there is little doubt that the well of competent engineers is drying up."
